text: The CV analogue of the Gottesman-Knill theorem says that circuits built only from Gaussian states, Gaussian operations, and Gaussian measurements are efficiently classically simulable. What does this imply for achieving a quantum computational advantage?
choices: Squeezing must exceed 15 dB before any Gaussian circuit becomes hard to simulate
Homodyne detection must be replaced by heterodyne detection
Some non-Gaussian element — e.g. photon-number-resolving detection, a cubic phase gate, or a GKP ancilla — must be injected
The circuit must use more than one million entangled modes
explanation: The no-go result means squeezers, beam splitters, and homodyne alone can never beat a classical computer; a non-Gaussian resource (cubic gate, photon counting, or GKP state) is mandatory. Choice 0 is false — no amount of squeezing makes a purely-Gaussian circuit hard; choice 1 is irrelevant (both are Gaussian measurements); choice 3 confuses entanglement scale with hardness (million-mode cluster states are Gaussian and simulable).
